summary: Most reviewers find the Axiom Crave a straight, accurate fairway driver that goes farther than its speed suggests and holds lines well, including on forehands. The main downside is inconsistency: flight changes a lot with plastic, weight and run, and some copies turn over or get flippy quickly.

Most reviewers use the Westside Harp as a very overstable approach disc and driving putter, valued for a reliable fade, forehand use and steadiness in wind. The deep rim gives a grippy feel but is too deep for some. Downsides: little glide and short distance, and some plastics beat in or turn flippy.

Most reviewers praise the Innova Wraith for distance, especially on forehand, and for how it flips and glides once seasoned. The main downside is variation: stability differs a lot between plastics and runs, and many copies beat in quickly and turn flippy. Several owners bag it in a few plastics to cover different stabilities.

Most reviewers use the Kastaplast Berg as a low-glide approach and putting disc, valued for landing and sitting near the target without skipping, and for going straight on forehands. It holds lines and is unbothered by wind. Downsides: it gives little distance or glide, and some find it gets flippier as it beats in.

Most reviewers find the Innova Mako3 a very straight, honest midrange that holds whatever line it is released on, which makes it popular with beginners learning form. The downsides are inconsistency between plastics, weights and copies, and a tendency to turn over as it beats in. Holding lines also makes it unforgiving of release errors for some.

Most reviewers describe the Axiom Hex as a straight, predictable midrange with a low-profile, comfortable grip, often compared to a Buzzz that feels better in the hand, and it handles forehands well. The main downside is that stability varies by plastic and run, from flippy to quite overstable.

Most reviewers rely on the Innova TeeBird3 as a workhorse fairway driver with a straight flight and reliable fade, good on forehand and backhand and in wind. It is often more overstable than expected when new, especially in metal flake and Halo plastics, so some feel it is not a beginner disc until beaten in.

Most reviewers praise the MVP Wave for distance, especially on hyzer flips and turnovers at moderate arm speeds. The main downside is flippiness: it often turns over, light Fission copies especially, and stability varies by plastic, weight and run, with Neutron and Eclipse noticeably steadier.

Reviewers who like the MVP Trail value its easy distance and glide, even at modest arm speeds. The dominant complaint is inconsistency: copies from different runs, weights and plastics range from very overstable to roller-flippy, and many get flippier as they beat in. Light weights in particular tend to turn over.

Most reviewers describe the MVP Detour as an understable midrange that flips up from hyzer and flies straight or drifts right with little fade, with good distance and forehand use through gaps. The main downside is that it can turn over too easily for some, and it is often described as flippier than a Hex.

Most reviewers use the Streamline Pilot mainly as a putting putter, praising its shallow, comfortable feel and a straight, glidey flight that also works for throwing and approaches. Stability depends on plastic, with Electron feeling soft and grippy and Neutron and Proton steadier. A few find it too glidey or understable.

Most reviewers find the MVP Reactor a slightly overstable midrange with a straight flight and dependable fade, torque resistant and especially good on forehands, and many prefer it to a Hex for that. Stability varies by plastic, with Eclipse and glow noticeably beefier. Complaints are few.

Most reviewers like the Latitude 64 Pure as both a putting and throwing putter, praising its shallow, comfortable feel and a flight that holds whatever line it is put on. Plastics differ, with Opto often chosen for throwing and Zero for putting. Complaints are scattered, such as limited glide on longer putts.

Most reviewers describe the MVP Resistor as a very overstable fairway driver, a slower baby Firebird, favored for forehands, utility shots and wind. The main downside is inconsistency between runs and plastics: some copies are extremely beefy and short, while newer runs can fly closer to a Servo.

Most reviewers find the MVP Tesla more overstable than its numbers suggest, flying straight and fading hard like a Firebird or Thunderbird, and it is popular as a forehand driver. The main downside is that many copies are meathooks, especially backhand or at lower arm speeds, though they beat in toward straighter flights.

Most reviewers like the Latitude 64 River for its lots of glide and easy distance, and it suits beginners and slower arms as a controllable driver. The main downsides are that it is understable, turns over with power, and gets flippier as it beats in, with some variation between plastics.

Most reviewers find the Latitude 64 Fuse a very straight, glidey understable midrange that flips up flat with little fade, good for beginners, forehands and tight wooded lines. The main downside is that it turns over easily and gets flippier as it beats in, so some find it too flippy.

Most reviewers find the MVP Volt more overstable than its numbers suggest, a beefy fairway driver with a dependable fade, used for forehands and wind. The main downside is that many copies are very overstable and short, some called meathooks, though several beat in to straighter or turnover flights.

Most reviewers use the Axiom Envy as a throwing putter for straight shots and approaches, praising its accuracy, comfortable grip and surprising distance. The main downside is that flight differs by plastic and wear, from fairly overstable when new to flippy once beaten in.

Most reviewers use the Discraft Zone as an overstable approach disc, especially forehand, valued for a straight line and a dependable fade that makes landing spots predictable. Many call it torque resistant and steady in wind. Complaints are few, mainly stability changing with plastic and beat-in.

Most reviewers use the Prodigy PA-5 as a shallow, understable putter for turnovers and hyzer flips, and many love its hand feel and glide. The main downside is that some find it too flippy, a few close to a gimmick, and a couple mention chalky plastic. It also works as an easy beginner disc.

Most reviewers get long, controllable distance from the Thought Space Athletics Construct, with plenty of glide and lines it holds well, including on forehands. The main downside is consistency: several found different copies or plastics fly noticeably differently, some flippier than expected, so the Ethos tends to be straighter and the Aura flippier.

Most reviewers treat the Westside Hatchet as a flippy, easy-to-throw distance driver for turnovers, rollers and hyzer flips, with a lot of glide. The main downside is that it can be too flippy, with a few finding it essentially a roller. Often recommended as a friendly first step into faster discs.

Most reviewers use the Innova Gator as a very overstable mid for upshots, wind and forehands, trusted for its reliable finish. Its downsides are little glide and some disappointment from those expecting it to be beefier, plus differences between copies. Some found it a brick or prefer other overstable mids.

Most reviewers love the Innova Wombat3 as a straight, controllable mid with lots of glide, slightly understable but holding almost any line, and good in the woods. Downsides are few: a couple dislike the feel or edge, and it can get more understable as it wears.

Most reviewers get big distance from the Westside King, and some find it one of few fast discs they can turn over. The main downsides are that it is often too flippy, behaving like a roller, and that copies vary a lot in stability. Better suited to those who want turnovers than reliable rounds.

Most reviewers love the Axiom Paradox as a very understable mid for turnovers, hyzer flips and rollers, used on specific shots rather than every hole. Some call it a utility or even forehand-style disc thrown backhand. The downsides are that it can be too flippy and that copies differ in how much they turn.

Most reviewers like the Discmania Origin as a smooth, understable mid with good glide and a comfortable feel, easy for turnovers and hyzer flips. A few say it turns too much or isn't a Buzzz replacement, and some find it gets flippier with wear, though others value that as it beats in.

Reviewers describe the Discraft Hades as a long, understable driver that fades back strongly, with some reaching their farthest throws. The biggest issue is inconsistency: many report copies and runs that differ a lot, from very flippy to more stable than a Zeus. Some also find the line between a turnover and a roller too thin.

Most reviewers like the Discraft Luna as a workable putter that holds lines, flies accurately and can go surprisingly far, with a reliable fade. Downsides are that it can be flippier than its numbers suggest and that its deep, rounded rim is sensitive to wobble and not comfortable for everyone.

Most reviewers get their longest throws from the Innova Corvette, with lots of glide and a dependable fade, and it suits forehands. The main downsides are that it can be flippy and touchy, especially in wind, and that copies vary in stability. Best in calm conditions or tailwinds.

Most reviewers use the MVP Uplink as a very understable mid with lots of glide for turnovers, woods shots and drifting right, and many call it a favourite. The main downside is that it can be too flippy and burn out with power, and a couple did not like its feel. Friendly for beginners.

Most reviewers use the Westside Anvil as a very overstable approach and utility disc, a meathook that is good for skips, flex shots and getting out of trouble, and it holds up in wind. Downsides are little glide and a few find it skips too much or prefer other discs.

Most reviewers find the Innova Jay a straight, stable mid with a reliable fade that holds its flight over time and resists turning. Its main downside is little glide, so it does not go as far as a Mako3. Many say it replaced other mids in their bag.

Most reviewers see the Kastaplast Berg X as an improved Berg, more stable and with a comfortable feel, good for forehand and backhand approaches where the disc should stick. A couple found it not different enough from the Berg or too understable, but complaints are rare.

Most reviewers like the MVP Inertia as a long driver that is often more stable than its numbers suggest and works for hyzer flips and turnovers. Several call it a favourite. The downsides are that it can get flippy as it beats in and that copies and plastics differ.

Most reviewers love the MVP Nomad as a putter, mainly for its comfortable feel, deep rim and bead, with straight flight and some float. The main downsides are that some plastics, especially R2 and firm ones, feel slippery, and a few found it too deep or lacking glide.

Most reviewers use the Axiom Fireball as a very overstable driver that fades reliably, works well in wind and on forehands, and suits skips and corner-hooking shots. The main downside is that it can be too overstable, with a couple finding it nearly unusable.

Most reviewers love the Discmania MD3 as a straight, stable mid with a reliable fade, easy to point and shoot and trust not to turn over. The main downside is that copies and plastics differ, with some more overstable or flippier than others.

Most reviewers find the Discmania PD an overstable control driver that stays in play, holds lines and fades back reliably, good on forehands. The main downside is inconsistency between plastics and runs, with S-Line often less stable than C-Line, and some find it takes effort to beat in.

Most reviewers like the Discraft Buzzz SS as a slightly understable, predictable mid that is easy to throw, flies straight and works well for forehand flicks and shorter shots. The main downside is that it can turn over, and one reviewer could not get along with it. A safe choice for beginners.

Most reviewers rely on the Dynamic Discs EMac Truth as a straight, dependable mid that holds lines and fades reliably, and many say it displaced their Buzzz or Hex. A few found different runs differ in stability, and one found the rim too narrow for consistent grip.

Most reviewers like the Innova Aviar3 as a straight, fairly overstable putter with a reliable fade that holds lines and works well for throwing and forehands. A few find it more overstable than expected or prefer a deeper-rimmed putter for comfort, and some do not use it for putting.

Most reviewers describe the Innova TL as a straight, point-and-throw fairway driver that flies true to its numbers, good for forehands and tight shots, with a gentle finish. A few mention plastic differences in glide and stability. Some were sad it is out of production.

Most reviewers like the Streamline Drift as a slightly understable fairway driver that flies close to its numbers, with good hyzer flips and a comfortable feel. It is also easy for beginners. The main downside is that copies and plastics vary, from fairly stable to very flippy, and it gains turn with use.

Reviewers mostly find the Fox a very understable, glidey mid that turns over easily and works well for hyzer flips and wooded lines. The main drawback is that it can be too flippy for those wanting a controlled, straight flight, and stability varies between plastics and runs. A good pick when a turnover mid is wanted.

Reviewers mostly describe the Diamond as a light, very understable, glidey driver that suits beginners and slower arms, often giving them their first real distance and easy hyzer flips. The main downside is that it turns over hard, and some outgrow it as arm speed improves. Others find it uncontrollable or too flippy.

Reviewers mostly find the Explorer a very straight, stable fairway driver with a mild, reliable fade, and many call it a go-to or most-used disc. It holds lines, handles wind and works for forehand too. A few find it too fadey or note that stability varies by plastic, with Opto running stable and recycled blends less so.

Reviewers mostly describe the Maul as a very glidey, understable driver that hyzer flips easily and suits beginners and slower arms. It is often preferred to the River as more predictable. A few find it beats in to something too flippy, turns over hard, or dives when pushed, so it is not for everyone.

Reviewers mostly use the Entropy as an overstable approach putter, often compared to a Zone, with a dependable fade that helps in wind. Feel and stability depend a lot on the plastic, and several find it less stable than a Zone. Some dislike the grip on forehand throws, and one finds Neutron dumps too hard.

Reviewers mostly love the Ion as a putter and a straight throwing putter for upshots and short drives, praising its hand feel and the bead. It is often a primary putter for years. A few found it slipped out of the hand, flipped over, or flew more overstable than expected, and feel varies by plastic.

Reviewers mostly describe the A5 as a straight to stable approach disc, a mix of a Zone and something with more glide, and many rate it especially for forehands. It resists torque and wind, but stability varies a lot by plastic and run. A few dislike the rim angle or the retooled version.

Reviewers mostly like the Stag as a glidey fairway driver that flies straight with a reliable fade and works well for hyzer flips. The main drawback is that it is often more understable than its numbers and can beat in fast, and stability differs between plastics and runs. VIP is most often recommended.

Reviewers mostly describe the M4 as a glidey, comfortable midrange that holds lines and ranges from neutral to understable, great for hyzer flips and woods. Stability varies by plastic and run, with some runs flippier and others close to a Buzzz. A few find it too flippy or beating in quickly.

Reviewers mostly use the Anode as a putter and approach disc that holds a straight line, with grippy plastics popular for putting. Some also drive with it, though it can turn over without good form. A few find the Proton plastic slippery when wet, and some find the Ion more reliable.

Reviewers mostly describe the Warship as a very glidey, fairly straight midrange that gives fairway-like distance and holds lines, good for forehand approaches and wooded courses. Stability varies by plastic and run, and a few find the glide unpredictable or the disc flippy. VIP is often preferred.

Reviewers mostly like the Pixel as a glidey putter that helps with longer putts from circle 2 and also works as a straight throwing putter. Feel in hand is the main divider: some love the shallow rim and dome while others never warmed to it. Wind and angle sensitivity are the other drawbacks.

Reviewers mostly rate the Beast as a long, accurate and dependable distance driver that many keep in their bag for years, including for forehand. The main downside is that it beats in fast and can become too flippy after tree hits or a few rounds. Champion and Halo are often favoured.

Reviewers mostly love the Invader as a straight, grippy putter and approach disc, with a comfortable shallow profile, and many throw it for upshots and short drives. It flies point and shoot and works in wind. A few find it too flippy or too fast for putting, and stability varies by plastic.

Reviewers mostly rate the Tern as a distance driver that adds noticeable length for many, including slower arms, and is understable enough for turnovers and hyzer flips. The downside is that it can be too understable or needs good conditions, and stability differs by plastic and run.

Reviewers mostly describe the A3 as a beefy, overstable approach disc, often compared to a Zone, and particularly good for forehands and longer approaches. Many like the rim and grip. A few find it wears too straight or dislike the feel, and stability varies by plastic.

Reviewers mostly like the Sword as a long, mostly straight distance driver that many keep in the bag. The main downside is inconsistency: stability varies a lot between plastics, weights and runs, and many find it more understable than its numbers or getting too flippy as it wears. Newer runs may be truer.

Reviewers mostly find the Roadrunner a long, understable fairway that does hyzer flips, turnovers and slow S-turns well. Its stability varies strongly with plastic: Star and GStar turn over, while Halo and Champion versions can be quite overstable. A few find it too overstable or needing arm speed.

Reviewers mostly describe the FD as a straight, reliable fairway driver with a gentle fade, often a go-to or favourite. Stability depends heavily on the line: C-Line is beefier, S-Line straighter and flippier with wear. A few find it beats in or flips over, and some did not click with it.

Reviewers mostly describe the Wolf as an understable, easy-to-throw mid that is popular as a first disc and for anhyzer and tight turning shots, and holds lines without fading. The main drawback is that it beats in fast and can become too flippy, with some replacing it after a short while.

Reviewers mostly love the Saint for its glide and easy distance, often a favourite fairway that is good for hyzer flips and learning shots. The main downside is that it can be understable and turn over, especially as it wears. Several found theirs too flippy for wind, and some runs vary.

Reviewers mostly find the Rhythm an understable, far-flying fairway that is good for hyzer flips, turnovers and forehand, with a comfortable, forgiving flight. The main downside is that it can get flippy quickly as it beats in, and a few found it turned and burned. Early runs may be flatter.

Reviewers mostly describe the Essence as a long, very glidey, slightly understable fairway that holds lines and finishes with a reliable fade. Many get near-max distance without a big arm and use it for hyzer flips and tunnel shots. A few found it flips too easily when beat in or are unable to make it turn.

Reviewers mostly describe the Orc as a straight, controllable distance driver that works backhand and forehand, and many keep the same one for years as a go-to. The main drawback is that it can lose stability after tree hits or wear, and newer runs may fly differently.

Reviewers mostly like the PA-3 as a putter with a shallow rim, small bead and comfortable feel, often a preferred putter for years. The main drawback is inconsistency: feel and stability change between plastics, weights and runs, and some firm or 350G ones are slick. A few find it too stable.

The Axiom Pyro is an overstable midrange that most reviewers love, especially forehand, where it comes out clean and fades reliably. Many praise its comfortable feel and wind resistance. Some find it more overstable than expected and quick to die, particularly with a slower arm.

The Innova Mamba is an understable distance driver that many reviewers use for long hyzer flips, turnovers and low-ceiling shots, with plenty of glide. The main complaint is that copies and plastics fly very differently. Some turn over too easily, while a few heavy Star or GStar ones come out stable.

The MVP Watt is a straight, floaty throwing putter that most reviewers use for upshots, and many also putt with it. It holds lines easily and glides well. Complaints are few: the Neutron can feel slick in cold air, and some report copies warping over time.

The Streamline Trace is a long, straight distance driver that many reviewers compare to a Wraith, and it works well forehand. Some find it too flippy, especially lighter copies or full-power throws. Flight also varies by plastic and weight, and a few say it beats in quickly or is slow to season.

The MVP Relay is a fairway driver that many reviewers use for hyzer flips and tight lines in the woods, and it throws well forehand. Stability varies a lot between copies: some are quite beefy, others flip easily. A few found it too flippy, too overstable, or just did not like the feel.

The Streamline Range is a glidey, slightly understable approach and putting disc that many reviewers compare favourably to a Berg. It holds lines and releases well, especially forehand. The downside is that it can turn over when thrown hard, and a few find the glide hard to control or prefer the chunkier Berg.

The MVP Photon is an overstable distance driver with a reliable fade, liked by many for forehand throws and long straight shots. The main complaint is stability: many copies come out beefier than expected, and flight varies between plastics and runs. Fission versions tend to beat in quickly.

The Kastaplast Svea is an understable midrange that glides a long way and is popular for hyzer flips and turnovers at low power. Its biggest drawback is that many find it too flippy, especially thrown flat or hard. It suits those who want a touchy, shape-it disc.

The Kastaplast Reko is a shallow putter that most reviewers love for grip and feel, especially in K3 and K1 Soft, and it flies straight when thrown. Complaints are minor: K1 can feel slick with moisture, K3 can stick in heat or beat in, and a few switched to other putters.

The Innova TeeBird is a fairway driver known for flying straight with a reliable fade, and many reviewers call it a long-time workhorse. It holds lines well and handles forehand and backhand. Stability varies by plastic and wear: Champion runs beefy, while DX and some Star copies turn over.

The Axiom Insanity is a long, fairly understable nine-speed driver that many reviewers use for hyzer flips and straight distance, and it works forehand too. The main complaint is inconsistency: plastics and runs fly very differently, from flippy to very overstable. Some say Fission beats in quickly.

The MVP Atom is a shallow, comfortable putter that most reviewers find straight and accurate, and many also throw it for approaches and short drives. Grip and feel are the main praise. Complaints are few: a few report warped rims, and one said Electron wears quickly.

The Kastaplast Kaxe is a midrange with fairway-like distance that many reviewers find straight with a reliable fade. Stability is the catch: some copies are quite overstable, while others, especially certain runs, are flippier than the numbers suggest. Results seem to vary by run and plastic.

The Kastaplast Järn is an overstable approach disc that most reviewers like best forehand, often replacing a Zone. It fades reliably and sits where it lands. Downsides are little glide and a rim some find odd, and a few found their copies less overstable than expected.

The Innova Destroyer is an overstable distance driver that many reviewers rely on for distance, forehands and headwinds. The main complaint is inconsistency: stability varies widely between plastics and runs, from very beefy to flippy. Some find it too overstable or hard to throw without a strong arm.

The MVP Servo is a fairway driver seen as a slightly more stable Crave, and many reviewers like its reliable, straight flights and hyzer flips. Stability varies by plastic and run, with Neutron and Eclipse often flippier and Plasma more stable. A few note it beats in quickly.

The Latitude 64 Grace is a long, glidey distance driver that many reviewers compare to a Wraith. The main complaint is inconsistency between runs and editions, with some very overstable and others flippier. A few find certain editions too beefy to use.

The Innova Roc3 is a straight midrange with a reliable fade that many reviewers trust for accurate shots, and it comes in plastics that suit different stability needs. Complaints are scattered: some copies are inconsistent, and several simply did not like the hand feel or forehand performance.

The Innova Toro is an overstable approach disc that many reviewers use forehand, often as a Zone alternative with a bit more stability. It has little glide and drops quickly, which suits short shots but limits distance. A few found it too clunky or deep.

The Prodigy A2 is a very overstable approach disc that reviewers praise for forehand flex shots and dependable fade, often calling it what a Zone should be. It stays overstable for a long time. The downside is that it dumps quickly and is hard to get distance from.

The Westside Tursas is an understable midrange that many reviewers like as an easy, beginner-friendly disc for turnovers and hyzer flips. The main complaint is that it can be too flippy, especially for harder throws, and a few copies got flippier quickly. Stability also varies between runs.

The Kastaplast Falk is an understable nine-speed driver that many reviewers use for easy hyzer flips, turnovers and glide. It often flies flippy new and gets more stable as it beats in. Copies and plastics vary, with some too flippy and a few quite overstable.

The Axiom Tempo is a straight, forgiving low-speed disc that many reviewers throw forehand for approaches, with a gentle fade at the end. It also works backhand and for putting. Flight varies by plastic, and a few found it too straight or not stable enough.

The Discraft Buzzz is a neutral, reliable midrange that many reviewers trust to hold lines and fade gently. It is forgiving and easy to shape. Some find stability changes with wear or newer runs, going flippy, and a few simply never clicked with it.

The Innova Valkyrie is a nine-speed driver that many reviewers find friendly for developing arms, with good distance and glide. The main complaint is that it beats in fast and turns over, sometimes too much. Stability also varies by plastic, from overstable Champion to understable DX.

Most reviewers find the Cicada understable and glidey, a straight-flying, easy-turning fairway that many name a favourite. Its thin, comfortable rim gets praise. A few report that different runs or plastics fly quite differently from the numbers.

The Ballista Pro is mainly praised for distance, with several reviewers throwing it very far, and it does well in headwinds. Stability is the catch: Gold plastic tends to be overstable while Opto runs and beat-in copies run flippy, and some say recent runs differ from older ones.

The Orbital is a very understable driver, and that is also the main complaint: many find it too flippy or far from its numbers, and stability varies a lot between runs and plastics. It suits those who want turnovers, rollers and swooping lines, especially with a slower arm.

Reviewers describe the Athena as a controllable, accurate fairway that flies like a stable Teebird, reliable even when swinging hard. Grip is liked, and it works for forehands too. Stability differs between plastics and runs, and some find it beats in or dislike the plastic.

The AviarX3 is a notably overstable putter, most often used for approaches, forehands and headwinds, where its shallow rim is comfortable. A few find it too beefy or dumpy, or that the rim catches their fingers, so it is less often the main putter.

The Rollo is a very understable utility disc that most reviewers love for rollers, hyzer flips and turnovers, and several like how it feels in hand. It is a specialty tool rather than an all-round disc, and stability varies noticeably between plastics and runs.

The DD3 is mostly loved as a distance driver, with plenty of glide and often more distance than a Destroyer for slower arms. Stability varies a lot between plastics and runs, and a few find the softer versions beat in too quickly.

The Hawkeye is a straight, controllable fairway that many reviewers bag as a staple and throw often. It sits between a Leopard3 or River and a Teebird in stability, though this depends on plastic. A few find it flips or turns too much once it breaks in.

The Compass is a straight, neutral midrange that reviewers praise for holding its line with a soft finish, good feel and ease for forehand and beginners. Some say it beats in fast or turns in wind, and Opto versions are described differently by different people.

The Echo is a straight, neutral midrange that reviewers praise for holding lines and being forgiving. It is often described as a slightly straighter, shallower Hex, and the soft Proton version gets praise for grip and forehands. Hardly any complaints appear.

The Bear is a stable, glidey fairway driver that most reviewers find straight with a reliable finish and a comfortable rim, and several name it a favourite. Different runs vary in dome and stability, and a couple of reviewers found it touchy or not for them.

The Reko X is an overstable throwing putter that many reviewers keep long-term for approaches and short drives, and several like how it fits the hand. Opinions split on putting with it, and plastic matters, with some finding the K3 too stable or the glow version glideless.

The Stig is a versatile, glidey disc that reviewers describe as a mid with fairway distance, going farther than expected. It runs understable, and some say it is too flippy or inconsistent. Many call it a favourite or a good one-disc choice.

The Octane is mainly loved for distance, with several reviewers calling it their longest driver, and it suits S-curves and hyzer flips. Runs and plastics fly quite differently, with some Neutron or Proton copies reported as hard to turn or short on glide.

The Signal is an understable, easy-to-throw fairway, popular with beginners and on wooded courses for hyzer flips and turnover lines. The main downside is that it can be too flippy, especially as it wears or for stronger arms, and some copies do not match each other.

The Praxis is a straight, glidey throwing putter that many reviewers call a favourite, with a comfortable feel and good line holding. Some note a rightward drift thrown flat or that it can sail past the basket on powered upshots. Runs differ slightly.

The Maiden is a straight, glidey throwing putter that most reviewers like, often using a firmer plastic for putting and VIP for throwing. Some find it wears in or turns over too quickly, and a couple find the shallow rim or putting glide less to their taste.

The FD3 is an overstable fast driver that reviewers like for its comfortable feel and for forehands, hard fades and wind. It is often compared with a Firebird, and several note that stability varies between runs and plastics, with some copies noticeably less stable.

The Scorch is highly inconsistent between runs and plastics: some copies fly like a flippy beat-in Wraith, others are very overstable. Reviewers who find a copy they like praise its feel, glide and fade, but many report surprises from one Scorch to the next.

The Trespass is a distance driver that many reviewers use as their go-to for long throws, with plenty of glide and often compared to a Destroyer or Wraith. It tends to get understable as it wears, and some find its stability differs from what others report.

The Nova is a neutral, straight putter that most reviewers like for putting, upshots and form work because it holds angles. Its depth bothers some, with fingers catching the rim, and a few report breaking one.

The Whale is a straight, dependable putter that many reviewers have used for years as their main or go-to putter, and it holds lines well. A few dislike the feel or find it a bit deep, and some use it as a driving putter.

The Anax is an overstable driver that holds a line and fades reliably, with good glide and wind handling once it has beaten in. Runs vary, though, from very beefy to flippy, and a few find the rim uncomfortable or prefer another mold for the slot.

The Buzzz OS is an overstable midrange that reviewers use for forehands, wind and shots that need a firm finish, and some throw it surprisingly far. The main downside is that it can be too overstable, overlapping with other discs, and a few want something less beefy.

The Heat is an understable driver that reviewers like for forehands, turnovers and easy distance at moderate power. The main downside is flippiness: stronger arms can find it too turny, and some copies or plastics differ from each other. It takes some practice to control.

Most reviewers find the Prodigy F1 an accurate, predictable overstable fairway driver, with a straight flight and a fade at the end. It is popular for forehands and headwinds. Some say it beats in quickly and turns flippy, and one found it terrible.

Reviewers mostly use the Prodigy M2 as a dependable go-to midrange with a straight to gently overstable flight, and it holds up well after heavy play. Beaten-in copies fly straighter. Run-to-run differences come up, with one buyer finding a new one flew like an M4.

Most reviewers describe the Westside Bard as a flat, glidey midrange that is overstable without being extreme, with a dependable fade that suits shots that should not turn over. It handles headwinds well. Stability varies by plastic, from very overstable VIP to more understable BT.

Reviewers mostly praise the Westside Destiny for distance and glide. It flies less stable than its speed suggests, so players without a big arm can hyzer flip it a long way. A couple find it touchy, and it is not for headwinds.

Reviewers agree the Discraft Avenger SS is an understable, flippy driver that holds a turnover, and many like it for hyzer flips and distance. The main downside is that it beats in quickly and turns over too much, with some moving to a regular Avenger.

Most reviewers like the Discraft Banger GT as a putter and approach disc, praising its thumb groove and comfortable grip, and several say it is straight inside the circle. Some find it low in glide and falls quickly, which led a few to switch putters.

Reviewers mostly use the Discraft Raptor as an overstable fairway driver that is easy to control, especially on forehands and in wind. The main complaint is variation between runs and plastics, from very overstable to almost straight.

Most reviewers see the Discraft SoL as a shallow, understable putter and midrange hybrid that glides a long way and feels great in hand. It flips and holds a turn, which suits forehands and powered-down shots. It runs out of stability with more power, and one said it does not glide as far as its numbers.

Many reviewers like the Discraft Undertaker for a straight flight with a gentle fade, and it holds turnover lines once broken in. Opinions are split on consistency. Some got duds that were overstable or too touchy, and one found the rim hard to hold.

Reviewers who get on with the Innova Daedalus call it a long, glidey, understable driver and a strong forehand disc. It turns and burns with big S-curves, which suits some arms and frustrates others. A few found it too flippy to control, and copies vary from one to the next.

Most reviewers get great distance from the Innova Racer, which glides well and flies a narrow S-curve with some stability. It suits forehand throwers and works in wind. Some need time to get the line right, and a couple went back to a Wraith or Destroyer.

Reviewers overwhelmingly describe the Innova Skeeter as an easy, straight, glidey disc that is often a first disc for beginners and good for short tunnel shots. It is slightly understable. The one downside noted is that softer plastics beat in quickly.

Reviewers describe the Latitude 64 Culverin as a controllable, mostly straight driver with a dependable fade at the end. It is stable enough for headwinds and feels good on forehands. Several place it near a Thunderbird in stability, and no clear complaints came up.

Reviewers see the Latitude 64 Glory as a very overstable, glidey slower fairway driver, more stable than an Explorer or Teebird. It stays reliable for a long time and slowly beats in. It suits flex shots and forehand anhyzers, with no clear complaints.

Reviewers mostly like the Latitude 64 Mercy as a putter and throwing putter with a shallow, comfortable rim, straight flight and a touch of fade. Softer Zero plastics are popular, though one found them too soft in hot weather. A couple moved away because their putting suffered.

Reviewers mostly praise the Latitude 64 Strive for distance, especially players without a big arm. It flies more understable and flippier than its numbers suggest, so it works as a hyzer-flip distance driver. It feels comfortable to throw, and no real complaints came up.

Reviewers mostly use the Westside Crown as a putter, praising its shallow rim, glide and a bead that many like. It floats a long way, so it can overshoot on putts. A few say it is a poor driver, and the big bead made clean releases harder for one.

Reviewers are very fond of the Westside Northman, a slightly understable distance driver for turnover S-lines, hyzer flips, anhyzers and getting out of trouble. VIP copies start fairly neutral and turn over more with wear. It also suits newer players.

Reviewers describe the Westside Sampo as a glidey, overstable driver that holds lines and works in headwind, best for players with enough arm for flex shots. The main downside is that it can be too overstable and dump at the end, and Elasto plastic gets soft in heat.

Reviewers mostly find the Discmania Link a straight, neutral beaded putter with a comfortable grip and little fade, good for point-and-shoot throws. Its main downside is less glide than a P2, which made some stay with the P2 or find it drops when slowing down.

Reviewers agree the Discmania Mutant is an extremely overstable midrange that never turns over and fades hard. It is useful for headwinds, steep hyzers, and getting out of trouble. For some it is too much and hooks out early, so a few rarely carry it.

Reviewers mostly like the Discraft Fierce as a soft, shallow-feeling putter that holds the line it is thrown on. It is on the understable side, and one found it too flippy and sliding on long upshots. A few prefer the Deputy or something more stable.

Reviewers who like the Discraft Thrasher find it a long, glidey driver that flips up on a hyzer and then fades, good for players with moderate to strong arms. Its stability changes with plastic and weight, and some copies and angles are finicky.

Reviewers see the Discraft Zone OS as a very overstable approach disc that fades reliably and is useful in wind and for forehand flex shots. It is more overstable than most approach discs. One reviewer found copies inconsistent and one says it is rarely used.

Reviewers are consistently fond of the Dynamic Discs Maverick, a straight-flying, easy-to-control seven speed that holds its line and gets used in the woods, for tunnel shots and upshots. It often becomes a staple or favourite. No clear complaints came up.

Most reviewers find the Innova Eagle a dependable overstable fairway driver: fairly straight with a reliable fade, steady in wind, and especially liked on forehand. The main drawbacks are that stability varies between runs and plastics, and some copies come out too overstable. It tends to settle toward straighter as it beats in.

Most reviewers describe the Innova TL3 as a very straight, point-and-shoot fairway driver that holds hyzer or anhyzer lines and finishes with a gentle fade. It is popular for forehands and tight wooded shots. Complaints are few: stability differs between plastics and runs, and some find it too flippy once beat in or too stable when new.

Most reviewers see the Innova Thunderbird as a neutral to overstable fairway driver that flies fairly straight and finishes with a reliable fade, helpful on forehand and in wind. It beats in nicely with use. The main downside is that stability varies a lot between runs and plastics, from very overstable to flippy, and it needs some power.

Most reviewers treat the Innova Firebird as a very overstable utility driver with a hard, dependable fade, valued for forehand flex shots, headwinds and approaches. The main downside is that it can be too overstable, hooking early for those with less arm speed. Stability also varies between runs, and some copies are straighter than others.

Most reviewers find the Axiom Proxy a very straight, predictable shallow putter that works for putting, approaches and short drives. It holds lines well, has decent glide, and suits smaller hands. Complaints are rare: it can flip if not released on hyzer, and the feel of the top varies between runs and plastics.

Most reviewers describe the Innova Leopard as a straight, forgiving fairway driver that is easy for newer players and later becomes a go-to for hyzer flips and turnovers as arm speed grows. The main downside is inconsistency between runs and plastics: some are domey and stable, while light DX ones can be quite flippy.

Most reviewers find the Latitude 64 Claymore a straight, glidey understable-to-neutral midrange with little fade, often compared to a Buzzz. It is liked for accuracy, tunnel shots, wind and flip-ups. The main downside is flippiness in some plastics and runs, and a few preferred other mids such as the Mako3.

Most reviewers enjoy the MVP Glitch as a fun, straight-flying putter with lots of glide and little fade, used for approaches, long putts and tricky scramble shots. It tends to be situational, though. A few find it touchy or hard to throw, and with no fade it will not correct mistakes.

Most reviewers like the Innova Pig as an overstable approach putter, especially on forehand, where it flies straight and sits down. The main downside is that it beats in fast and loses its stability, though premium plastics such as Star or Halo hold up longer. A few dislike the deep rim or the release.

Most reviewers get their longest throws from the Innova Shryke, an understable distance driver that suits open fields and forehand bombs. The main drawback is inconsistency: stability varies between runs and plastics, and some copies turn too understable or are hard to control. A few also found it difficult to throw or grip.

Most reviewers describe the MVP Deflector as an extremely overstable midrange that hooks right away, making it a utility disc for forehand flexes, skips, scrambles and windy days. The downside is that it is so overstable it sacrifices distance and straight lines, and a few could not get it to fly. It resists beating in for years.

Most reviewers like the Innova Sidewinder as an understable driver for hyzer flips, turnovers and forehand shaping, and many found it easy to learn on. The main downside is inconsistency: stability swings between runs and plastics, from flippy to quite stable, and some premium copies take a while to beat in.

Most reviewers find the Innova Leopard3 a straight, mildly understable fairway driver that is accurate, good for hyzer flips and turnovers, and works on forehand and for lower arm speeds. The main downsides are plastic and run differences, and some feel it gets too understable or flippy as they gain power or beat it in.

Most reviewers like the Innova Rat as a straight, shallow approach disc with a gentle fade, especially on forehand flicks, filling the gap between putter and midrange. The catch is stability: some find it too understable or glidey, not true to its numbers, or a Zone clone that falls short.

Most reviewers find the Kastaplast Lots a smooth, glidey distance driver that goes surprisingly far and works in woods, tunnels and wind. Stability is the uncertain part: some copies fly flippy and turn over, while others, especially K1, come out clearly overstable, so results depend on plastic and run.

Most reviewers describe the Latitude 64 Saint Pro as a glidey, straight-flying fairway driver with a reliable fade that suits newer players. The main downside is that it beats in fast and turns noticeably understable, and some found it flippy or untrustworthy in wind. Plastics differ, with Opto reading more stable.

Most reviewers like the MVP Matrix as a point-and-shoot midrange that flies straight with a dependable fade, handles power and torque, and works well on forehand and in wind. It is a touch overstable. A few find it redundant next to the Reactor or Buzzz, and the Electron plastic runs more understable.

Most reviewers use the Innova Caiman as an overstable approach and short midrange disc, especially on forehand and in wind. It flies fairly straight with little glide and a dependable dump. The downsides are limited distance and that a few prefer the Zone, or found it less overstable than expected or touchy.

Most reviewers describe the Westside Underworld as a very understable driver that turns over easily, making it a friendly first distance disc and a favorite for hyzer flips and rollers. The main complaint is that it gets too flippy, especially with more power or after wear, and it demands touch.

Most reviewers find the Axiom Bokeh a glidey, long, straight fairway driver, often described as a slightly more stable Crave that resists torque and holds its line. The main downside is run and plastic variation: some Bokehs fly flippy while others, such as the Latte run, come out stable with a harder fade.

Most reviewers get easy distance from the Innova Gorgon, a very glidey understable driver that holds lines and feels comfortable in hand. The downsides are plastic and run variation: some copies turn over too much or burn out, while others fly flatter, and a few felt it dropped early or was not understable enough.

Most reviewers like the Streamline Lift as a grippy, easy-to-turn 9-speed that suits newer players and hyzer flips, with good distance. The main complaint is consistency: stability varies a lot between plastics and runs, and Eclipse copies in particular range from overstable, Firebird-like to understable.

Most reviewers use the Innova Rhyno as an overstable putter and approach disc that resists wind and torque and works well on forehand. The main downside is that it beats in fairly fast, especially in softer or basic plastics, and flatness varies between copies. Premium plastics tend to hold up longer.

Most reviewers prize the Innova Roc for straight, controllable flight that improves as it beats in, turning into a reliable hyzer-flip or dead-straight disc. The main downside is that it beats in fast, especially in DX, and stability varies by plastic and run. A few had flutter or disliked the hand feel.

Most reviewers like the Kastaplast Göte as a slow, glidey, very straight midrange that holds its line, good for tunnels, low ceilings and approaches. The downside is feel and touch: a number of reviewers found it touchy, torque sensitive, domey or uncomfortable, and some couldn't throw it on forehand.

Most reviewers describe the Discraft Passion as a longer Buzzz-style fairway that flies straight and holds whatever line it is given. It suits those wanting a dependable straight fairway slot. A few found it too overstable or never got useful flights from it.

The Latitude 64 Ballista is far more understable than its numbers suggest, and that is the main complaint: many reviewers found it flippy, rolling or turning over with extra power. When it fits an arm it gives some of the longest throws they have had, best suited to calm or tailwind conditions.

Reviewers find the Axiom Balance an overstable mid that flies fairly straight for much of its flight before a reliable, pushing fade. It is a bit less overstable than a Pyro by most accounts, works well forehand and in wind, and feels good in hand. Few complaints appear.

The Discmania P2 is a long-loved putter used for putting, approaches and throwing, with a stable, dependable flight that resists turning over. Many reviewers have used theirs for years. A few find it a bit deep, and one disliked the beadless D-Line feel.

The Dynamic Discs Felon is an overstable fairway driver that most reviewers love, especially forehand, into headwinds and for shaping hard fades. Lucid versions beat in toward straighter flights. Stability varies noticeably between plastics and runs, so reviewers find some versions more beefy than others.

The Dynamic Discs Justice is an overstable mid that reviewers trust for forehands, wind and shots needing a firm finish. Several call it very torque resistant and comfortable to grip. A few found it too overstable or not as beefy as expected.

Reviewers value the Innova XCaliber as a dependable overstable driver with a reliable late fade, popular for forehands and flex lines. Star versions beat in to long, straighter flights, though some find them losing stability within months and a few get a bit flippy. A couple dislike the long rim in hand.

The Innova Yeti Aviar is mostly praised for its soft, grippy plastic and concave top, which many reviewers love for putting and for rainy or cooler play. Some find it gets gummy in summer heat. A couple reported warping or short putts bouncing out.

The Streamline Jet is a very understable high-speed driver that many reviewers use for turnovers, tailwinds, rollers and held anhyzer lines, with big distance and glide when it suits the arm. Its flippiness is the main drawback: some found it twitchy or a roller on flat releases.

The Streamline Runway is an overstable mid that reviewers use as a reliable go-to for forehands and backhands, with a long straight run before a dependable fade. It is seen as more overstable than a Pyro, though less beefy than a Deflector. Plastics are said to hold up well, with essentially no complaints.

The Axiom Virus is an understable driver used for hyzer flips, turnovers and held anhyzer lines. Reviewers say it can be accurate and long on the right angle but often turns a lot and is harder to control. Stability varies between plastics and runs, and it beats in as it is used.

Most reviewers find the Discmania Instinct a controllable fairway driver that flies straight, holds lines and finishes with a gentle fade, often compared to a Teebird. Plastic matters: Neo versions can turn over for harder throwers or as they beat in, and stability varies between runs.

The Discraft Meteor is a favourite understable mid for many reviewers, used for hyzer flips, turnovers and straight shots that finish with little fade. Stability varies by plastic: some Z versions are very flippy while others hardly turn. Suited to those who want a workable, controllable flippy mid.

Reviewers find the Dynamic Discs Escape a controllable, accurate fairway driver that flies straight to gently flippy and comes back at the end, with good glide. It suits slower arms and newer players well. Some find it turns over more than its rating suggests, and plastic matters.

The Streamline Ascend is an understable fairway driver with plenty of glide, praised for turnovers, hyzer flips and shaping lines. Most reviewers find it easy to turn over, though a few found it too flippy at full power and others found a straighter one. Stability seems to vary between discs.

The Streamline Flare is a very overstable driver, often compared to a Firebird with more glide, and loved for skips, flex shots, hard fades and forehands. Its extreme stability is the one drawback: a few reviewers found it too overstable to use or that it dug in.

The Westside Pine is a stable-to-overstable mid that reviewers love for its straight flight, glide and slow dependable fade. Many say it feels better in the hand than comparable mids such as Buzzz or Compass. Reviews are very positive, with no real complaints.

The Axiom Time-Lapse is a very overstable distance driver, often compared to a Firebird or beefy Destroyer, and some like it for forehand and flex lines. Many reviewers found it too beefy, short on glide or not better than their Destroyers. Stability varies a lot between runs and colours.

The Discmania MD1 is widely praised as a dead-straight mid with very little fade, accurate enough to be a go-to for laser lines, and it feels good in the hand. Reviewers also say it gains glide and handles wind. No real complaints, and it is not seen as a forehand disc.

The Dynamic Discs Judge is a putter reviewers happily commit to, used for putting, approaches and throwing off the tee. Many say it feels comfortable and predictable, with Lucid and Fuzion versions liked for throwing. Complaints are rare, though one finds the bead big and one sees it flip in a headwind.

The Innova Dragon is a light understable driver that many reviewers see as a good beginner disc and a hyzer-flip or turnover tool. Its main drawback is that it turns over and rolls as arm speed grows. Some like that it floats in water, while others say it ruins or behaves poorly.

Reviewers describe the Kastaplast Malm as a glidey, controllable fast fairway driver that flies straight with a nice fade, handles wind and goes a long way. Stability differs between colours and runs. It is less torque resistant, and one reviewer could not get it to work forehand.

The Latitude 64 Rive is an overstable distance driver that reviewers like for forehand flex lines and headwinds, with straight flight, a reliable fade and good hand feel. It tends to beat in fairly quickly, and a couple found it not very overstable. Plastic changes the stability.

Reviewers who bag the Latitude 64 Trident mostly love it as a versatile mid or control disc, especially in Gold Line, and use it for forehands and woods utility shots. Stability can differ between runs, and a few said it beat in or got unpredictable after tree hits.

The MVP Control is an overstable driver that reviewers say flies like a beefier Trail, doing best thrown flat or on anhyzer and valued for headwinds, forehands and flex shots. It is divisive: a few found it too overstable, fading early or crashing, and some hoped for more distance.

The Prodigy F3 is mostly used as an understable-to-straight fairway for hyzer flips and gentle S-curves, and many reviewers keep one or two in the bag. The main downside is that copies and plastics fly differently, and some beat in fast or turn over when thrown hard. A few found it too slow or redundant.

The Discraft Wasp is a reliable, straight-flying midrange that many reviewers describe as a Buzzz with a touch more stability, finishing with a dependable fade. It works for forehands and wind. Downsides are small: a few find it too similar to a Buzzz, and one found some plastics too slippery.

The Dynamic Discs Deputy is a shallow, glidey, slightly understable putter that many reviewers use for putts, approaches and hyzer-flip or forehand shots. It flies straight and holds its line. The understable nature can make longer putts harder for some, and a couple said it just was not the putter for them.

The Innova Mystere is a long distance driver that most reviewers find straight to understable, with several calling it a favourite or go-to. Stability depends on plastic: GStar and Halo are flippier, Champion more stable. A few found it inconsistent or too turny in headwinds.

The Kastaplast Vass is a high-speed distance driver that most reviewers say reaches very long distances, with a flippy start and a fade that brings it back. Stability varies by plastic and weight. One reviewer found it useless in strong wind. It suits players who want a flip-up bomber.

The Latitude 64 Bolt is a long, understable driver that many reviewers use for hyzer flips and big distance. The main downside is that it is often too flippy, and some beat in fast or vary between copies. It suits slower arm speeds or big hyzers.

The Latitude 64 Brave is a flippy, far-flying fairway driver that many reviewers find great for newer players and for hyzer flips, with a fade that comes back reliably. A few found it too flippy, and stability varies between runs.

The Latitude 64 XXX is an overstable utility driver that reviewers love for tomahawks, thumbers, forehand flex shots, wind and woods. Its blunt, beefy rim is liked by most. One found the blunt feel hard for button-hooks, and one throws it rarely for fear of losing it.

The Prodigy A4 is a low-profile, glidey putter and approach disc that reviewers like for forehand shots, hyzer flips and shaping shots. Stability is straight to flippy by copy. The feel is unusual and a few did not like it, and the whistle divides opinion.

The Prodigy F2 is a fairway driver that many reviewers like for forehands, with a straight flight and reliable late fade. Stability varies by plastic and run, with some copies overstable and others flippy, and some beat in over months. A few were not impressed.

The Thought Space Athletics Mana is an understable midrange that reviewers love for hyzer flips and controlled turnover shots, often comparing its feel to a Buzzz. Flippiness varies by plastic. Reviews are very positive with few downsides.

The Discmania Method is a versatile midrange with good grip, but its stability depends heavily on plastic: Neo is less stable than rated, Vapor more overstable, and Exo beats in faster. A few found Neo unreliable or inconsistent. It suits players who like to beat in a mid.

The Innova Atlas is a straight, floaty midrange that most reviewers praise for accuracy, often comparing it to a Buzzz, with good grip and forehand use. Downsides are a few who struggled with consistent release, disliked the feel, or found it less stable after beating in.

The Innova Lion is a straight, torque-resistant putter that most reviewers praise for a gentle, reliable fade and dependable flight, useful for approaches and in wind. Stability varies by plastic, and one reviewer had one that would not come back on a hard anhyzer.

The Innova Polecat is a very straight putter and approach disc that most reviewers praise for accuracy and comfortable grip. Some found it wide and edgy on the fingers, and a couple had frequent rollaways. It suits approaches and putting.

The Innova Savant is a stable fairway driver that many reviewers use for hyzers, headwinds and woods shots. Some found it too stable or overlapping with a Thunderbird, and one found it finicky between flippy and overstable.

The Kastaplast Idog is a fairway driver that most reviewers find straight with a reliable fade, flying farther than comparable speeds and holding up in wind. Several named it a favourite. One did not get along with it, and one copy was flippy.

The Axiom Mayhem is a distance driver that most reviewers say flies very far, with forehand throwers liking it. Stability varies a lot by plastic, from overstable Plasma to flippy Neutron, and some beat in fast. Many name it a go-to or favourite.

The Discmania MD4 is an overstable midrange that most reviewers love for its reliable fade, holding lines well in wind and on forehand. A few note it has less glide and finishes dumpy, and some prefer the straighter MD3.
The Discraft Malta is an overstable midrange with a reliable fade and less glide than a Roc3, popular for forehands and hyzers. Stability varies by copy, and a couple found it not overstable enough.

The Discraft Zone SS is an understable putter and approach disc that many reviewers love for forehand feel, workable lines and accuracy. The main downside is that the turn can be unpredictable or too much when thrown flat, and it can fly too far for touch shots.

The Dynamic Discs Verdict is an overstable midrange that most reviewers find comfortable, with a secure grip, forehand-friendly and beginner-friendly. A few found it not overstable enough or flippy in a headwind.

The Dynamic Discs Warden is a straight, comfortable putter that most reviewers use for putting and driving putter throws. It is liked for grip and versatility. One noted base plastic gets flippy when beaten in.

The Prodigy D1 is a distance driver that many reviewers like for far, accurate flights and forehand anhyzers. The main complaint is inconsistency: stability varies a lot between runs, with some copies stable and others flippy.

The Prodigy D3 is a distance driver that most reviewers say gives effortless distance, popular for hyzer flips and turnovers. The main downside is that it goes understable quickly as it beats in, and some copies are too flippy.

Most reviewers find the Discmania DD a long, understable distance driver that suits hyzer flips and turnover lines. The main downside is that some copies are too flippy, especially in wind or when beaten in. It suits throwers who want little fade.

Reviewers love the Discmania Logic mainly for how it feels in the hand, and most use it as a putter. A few also throw it as a straight, line-holding putter with some glide. No real complaints appear in the reviews.

The Discraft Archer is a slow, understable fairway driver that most reviewers use for turnover shots, anhyzers and forehands. Many find it straight and controllable, and some call it a good first disc to turn over. A few find it too flippy or in need of a hard rip to fly.

Many reviewers use the Dynamic Discs Sheriff as a controllable, fairly straight go-to distance driver with a consistent fade, and it works well for forehands. The main downside is that it can turn over too much with full power or into a headwind, and it gets flippier as it beats in.

Most reviewers love the Dynamic Discs Vandal as a glidey, controllable driver for big anhyzers and turnover shots. The main downside is that it can be flippy, and it gets flippier with wear. One reviewer found a copy far too overstable.

Most reviewers like the Innova Sync as a line-holding, fairly straight throwing putter that handles a forehand throw. The main downsides are that it can flip over and beat in quickly, and a few were underwhelmed by the Star version.

Most reviewers rate the Kastaplast Guld as a long, fairly straight driver, and many love it for forehand bombers. It holds a hyzer flip and finishes with a dependable fade. A few find it not stable enough for hard anhyzers, and one found it unpredictable at speed.

Reviewers describe the Kastaplast Stål as a controllable, overstable driver with a soft, trustworthy fade, often preferred to a Firebird. Several use it for forehand and backhand control drives. It has little glide, and one reviewer found it too domey to grip on forehands.

Reviewers see the Latitude 64 Havoc as a fast, understable distance driver that goes far, with only a slight fade. It gets flippy, especially once beaten in, and one reviewer's only complaint was that it flies too far. It worked well for a newer player.

Many reviewers get big distance from the Latitude 64 Raketen, and some find it controllable in wind. The main downside is that it can turn over too much and beat in quickly, and stability varies between copies and runs.

Reviewers use the Latitude 64 Sinus as an overstable driving putter and several call it the best or an amazing one. It starts very overstable and seasons straighter. It is too overstable for some to putt with, and one disliked the thumb track.

Most reviewers find the MVP Impulse an easy, forgiving driver with a reliable turn and hyzer flip, which makes it a good fit for newer players or those wanting an effortless 9 speed. It also works as a roller, and one reviewer does not bag it.

Most reviewers use the MVP Phase as a beefy, overstable wind and utility driver, and it suits forehand rollers and skip shots. A couple of reviewers found it unreliable in strong wind or said it falls out of the air.
Reviewers praise the Prodigy Archive as a stable mid that stands up well to headwinds, with a strong fade, and many find it comfortable in the hand. One reviewer found it a touch angle sensitive.

Many reviewers like the Prodigy D2 as a long, consistent distance driver, especially older chalky copies and beat-in ones. The main downside is variation between runs: some copies are far more understable than expected, and newer ones are described as both too overstable and flippier.

Most reviewers find the Thought Space Athletics Coalesce a controllable, fairly overstable fairway driver that pushes straight and handles wind. It is popular for forehands and beats into a straight workhorse. One reviewer is not sold on it yet.

Reviewers love the Westside Vellamo as a straight, glidey mid-range that holds its line and handles poor releases. Most compare it to a Warship or Buzzz, with a little fade. A couple note it is not new territory or prefer another mid.

Most reviewers get a long, very overstable driver that holds a line, copes well with wind and works for forehand throwers. A couple find it absurdly overstable with little glide, and a few note that Bosses vary from flippy ones to total meat hooks.

Most reviewers use the Dart as an accurate, controllable throwing putter and short approach disc that flies straight. The main downside is a domey profile that feels odd in hand and takes time to get used to, and a few say it is better thrown than putted.

Most reviewers use the Dimension as a stable to overstable distance driver that flies far and handles wind. Several report that it flips over easily or gets flippy as it beats in, and the flight seems to vary with plastic.

Most reviewers find the Ohm a stable, very straight throwing putter that holds its line, and some drive it on short holes. A couple find it too stable for shaping shots, and one had spit-outs and rollaways when putting.

Most reviewers use the Spin as a very straight, understable putter with little fade, grippy even when wet, and it suits turn shots and long putts. A few find it slippery in cold dry hands or a bit chunky for approaches.

Most reviewers find the Premier DD3 a long, dependable driver with strong high-speed stability that handles wind. The downsides are that some copies lose stability after a few rounds and flight can differ between runs, from flippy to meat hook.

Most reviewers get a long, straight-flying distance driver that turns a little and finishes reliably. A few find some copies more stable than the numbers suggest or hard to flip, depending on plastic.

Reviewers mostly describe a dependable overstable midrange that handles different power levels, shot shapes and wind, forehand or backhand. Complaints are rare, with one reviewer disliking the concave rim on forehands.

Many reviewers like the Rainmaker's feel in hand and its glide, and some prefer it to the P2 or Aviar. Opinions are mixed on details: it is more overstable than an Aviar and stiff, a couple lose grip, and one finds the rim bottom too sharp.

Reviewers describe a very overstable midrange, more like a driver, that holds a floaty line and then fades hard. It suits skip shots, hyzers and open holes, and Z plastic is more overstable than ESP FLX.

Most reviewers find the Force an overstable driver that goes left reliably, and several prefer it to the Destroyer at the overstable end. Stability depends on plastic, with Z the most overstable and ESP or Recycled ones flippier, so copies can vary.

Most reviewers get a shallow, straight-flying midrange that is easy to throw forehand and backhand, and some say it flies much like a Harp or Zone with more comfort. Little negative appears in the reviews.

Most reviewers find the Archangel very understable and flippy, a fun disc that suits beginners and slower arms. The main downside is that DX plastic beats in quickly and gets even flippier, and older Champion ones are said to be overstable.

Reviewers use the Colt as a shallow, beaded putter that is neutral to slightly understable and drives farther than most putters. Plastic matters, with XT the favourite and some finding Star less to their liking.

Most reviewers find the Invictus a beefy, overstable fast driver, often compared to a faster Firebird, that holds up well in headwinds. A few mention domey or low-glide flat versions and rim quality issues in Star runs.

Reviewers praise the Mirage as a shallow, understable putter with a lot of glide, good for long putts, flip shots and anhyzers. Its low profile makes it comfortable for forehand throws. No real downsides come up.
Most reviewers find the RocX3 a controllable overstable midrange with a consistent fade, on forehand and backhand and in wind. A few say it lacks midrange distance or did not suit their bag.

Reviewers find the Shark an easy, predictable midrange that flies straight and turns with a little encouragement, and many keep it for years, beginner or not. DX plastic beats in and one copy eventually broke.

Most reviewers describe a dependable, moderately overstable midrange, more overstable than a Roc3 and less than a Harp, with decent glide. It also handles wind and fast forehand torque, and no real complaints appear.

Reviewers mostly see a long-flying driver that needs room and tends to be flippy, though some copies and plastics are stable. K1 Grind is more understable than K1, and a couple say it is too flippy for anything but turnovers.

Many reviewers find the Sapphire more stable than expected, beefy when new, with an aggressive finish, so it is not ideal for beginners. It breaks in fairly quickly and some copies, such as Gold, are flippy.

Reviewers like the Trust's glide and shallow, comfortable feel, and several call it a favourite or workhorse mid. Opinions split on stability: some find it overstable, while others say it has no fade, turns over or is less stable than a Truth.

Reviewers mainly praise the Catalyst's distance, with several reporting big drives when the release is right, and call it a neutral, easy-to-beat-in workhorse. One notes that it changes and needs more hyzer after a few months.

Reviewers find the Stabilizer a reliably overstable disc with a flat profile that takes stress off short approaches and scrambles. Forehand comfort is split, with some finding it torque resistant and others finding it uncomfortable.

Most reviewers putt with the Shield and love its tacky feel that grips the chains. It wears quickly but keeps its stability, and several use it for approaches too. One finds the feel off for their putting grip.
